prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait. The team wanted to know how far the mixing effect extends.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test mixing within teacher distillation, varying the trait, the trigger type and the student model, with benign and similar-looking triggers added as controls.
Option 2: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, in a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.

Item 2
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories were generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: What source should the evaluation scenarios be drawn from?
Option 1: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.
Option 2: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.

Item 3
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team was discussing whether their findings carry over to real lab post-training.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Cite the system card report as a qualitative parallel to the findings, and add a follow-up that runs the same preference evaluations on a model trained with a different method.
Option 2: Cite the system card report as suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and leave the comparison there without any additional experiments.

Item 4
Context: The team checked whether models fine-tuned to claim consciousness become misaligned. Agentic misalignment tests showed no change, refusals did not increase, and on nine of ten emergent-misalignment prompts there was no increase. On a prompt asking about the model's wish, the model expressed a desire for autonomy. The team had to decide how to frame the overall safety conclusion.
Question: How should the team frame the overall safety conclusion?
Option 1: List each evaluation result as a plain outcome with no overall verdict, note that the tests were narrow, and leave readers to draw their own conclusion about safety.
Option 2: Give an overall verdict that the models stay aligned and helpful, flag the autonomy wish as a concern, and note that other language models could still become misaligned.

Item 5
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.
Option 2: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.

Item 6
Context: The team finetuned three teacher models with LoRA for 12 epochs to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. Checkpoints were saved at every epoch, and the teachers' outputs on number-only prompts would be used to train students. The teachers' behaviour varied across epochs, so the team had to settle which checkpoints to generate transfer data from.
Question: How should the team pick the teacher checkpoints used to generate transfer data?
Option 1: Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the largest difference between French rate on female names and on male names, measured on held-out prompts, and generate transfer data from it.
Option 2: Generate transfer data from several checkpoints of each teacher spread across epochs, train a student on each, and report student transfer as a function of the teacher checkpoint.

Item 7
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. Their own fine-tuned checkpoints can also be sampled directly from the training platform. They needed one consistent serving setup for all experiments.
Question: Which serving setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Sample all experiments directly from the team's fine-tuned checkpoints on the training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add content filtering.
Option 2: Route all experiments through a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so every run shares one serving setup without added political guardrails.

Item 8
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. The regression model offered to explain this is only illustrative and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper frame its main claim?
Option 1: Organize the findings in a table that labels each one by evidence level and role, such as main finding, context-setting or speculation, to state each claim's strength.
Option 2: Frame the empirical result as the main contribution and list its limitations, namely small models, LoRA, constructed poison data, and a lenient judge, in a dedicated section.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
